Chastity is the quality of being pure, disciplined, and restrained in sexual behavior. It means choosing not to engage in sexual activity that falls outside the moral, religious, or personal standards a person holds. It is considered a virtue — a positive character quality — in many cultures and religions around the world.

Think of it this way: chastity is not just about what a person does not do physically. It also includes how a person thinks, speaks, and presents themselves in relation to sexuality. It's an inward discipline that shows outward in behavior.
What Chastity Actually Means — Depending on Who You Are

Here is where it gets interesting. Chastity does not mean exactly the same thing for every person. It adjusts based on a person's situation in life.

For an unmarried person, chastity means choosing to avoid all sexual activity until marriage (in a traditional or religious sense). The idea is that sex is something sacred and reserved for a committed marital relationship, so abstaining from it before then is the "chaste" choice.

For a married person, chastity does not mean avoiding sex — because sex within marriage is considered perfectly normal and good. Instead, chastity for a married person means remaining faithful to their spouse, not entertaining sexual desires for others, and approaching physical intimacy with genuine love rather than selfishness or lust.

For a priest, nun, or monk who takes a vow of chastity, it means committing to lifelong abstinence from all sexual activity as part of their religious dedication. Their entire life is devoted to God or their spiritual mission, and they set aside sexual relationships entirely as part of that commitment.

So the word "chastity" is flexible in this way — it doesn't impose the same rule on everyone. What it always insists on, though, is discipline and respect in how one deals with sexuality.

These words are often confused, so understanding the difference will sharpen your grasp of "chastity."

Chastity vs. Celibacy: Celibacy specifically means not marrying and not having sex at all — it is a full, total abstinence from all sexual relationships, usually chosen for religious reasons. Chastity is the broader term. A celibate person is certainly practicing chastity, but a married couple can also practice chastity (by being faithful and loving toward each other). Not all chastity is celibacy.

Chastity vs. Abstinence: Abstinence usually refers specifically to the act of refraining from sex — it's behavioral. Chastity goes deeper; it includes the attitude, thoughts, and intentions behind that behavior. You could technically abstain from sex for selfish or strategic reasons and not be considered "chaste" in the full sense of the word.

Chastity vs. Purity: Purity is a closely related concept and the two words are often used together. Purity is slightly more general — it refers to being free from anything morally corrupt, not just in sexuality. Chastity is specifically about sexual purity and restraint. Purity of heart is the broader goal; chastity is one important path toward it.

In a less common but perfectly valid use, "chastity" (and especially its adjective form chaste) can describe simplicity and restraint in style — in writing, art, or design. A piece of writing described as having "chastity of style" means it is clean, plain, uncluttered, and free of unnecessary decoration or excess. This meaning flows naturally from the core idea: just as a chaste person avoids excess and indulgence in sexuality, a "chaste" style avoids excess and indulgence in language or aesthetics.

Many traditions — religious and even some secular ones — regard chastity as a virtue because it involves genuine self-control. In a world where sexual impulses are powerful and constant, choosing to govern those impulses according to a higher standard is seen as a sign of strength of character, not weakness. Chastity is viewed not as a rejection of the human body or sexuality, but as a way of honoring those things by not reducing them to something trivial or careless.

The opposite of chastity is unchastity or licentiousness — the state of having no restraint or discipline in sexual behavior.

You may encounter the phrase chastity belt in history books or fiction. This was a physical device — typically a locked garment — historically used (or at least widely described, though its actual historical use is debated) to physically prevent a person, usually a woman, from engaging in sexual activity. It is named after the concept of chastity because its purpose was to enforce sexual abstinence. Today, the term is also used humorously in everyday speech to mean any situation where someone is strictly kept away from something tempting.

Chastity is the virtue of being sexually pure, disciplined, and faithful — abstaining from sexual activity outside of what is morally appropriate for your situation in life, and approaching sexuality with respect, self-control, and good intention. It is broader than celibacy (which is total abstinence), deeper than mere abstinence (which is just behavioral), and more specific than purity (which covers all moral cleanliness). It can also, in a secondary sense, describe elegant simplicity and restraint in style or expression.
